definition: In linguistics and language technology, a language resource is a "[composition] of linguistic material used in the construction, improvement and/or evaluation of language processing applications, (...) in language and language-mediated research studies and applications." According to Bird & Simons (2003), this includes data, i.e.
details: "any information that documents or describes a language, such as a published monograph, a computer data file, or even a shoebox full of handwritten index cards. The information could range in content from unanalyzed sound recordings to fully transcribed and annotated texts to a complete descriptive grammar", tools, i.e., "computational resources that facilitate creating, viewing, querying, or otherwise using language data", and advice, i.e., "any information about what data sources are reliable, what tools are appropriate in a given situation, what practices to follow when creating new data". The latter aspect is usually referred to as "best practices" or "(community) standards". In a narrower sense, language resource is specifically applied to resources that are available in digital form, and then, "encompassing (a) data sets (textual, multimodal/multimedia and lexical data, grammars, language models, etc.) in machine readable form, and (b) tools/technologies/services used for their processing and management".

explainer.lead: A language resource is linguistic material used to build, improve or evaluate language processing applications and language research. It matters because data, tools and guidance determine what language systems can be trained and tested on.

tiers.eli5: It's the raw material and toolbox for language work — recordings, transcripts, grammars, and notes on which sources you can trust.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers assemble corpora, annotation tools and guidance on source reliability before training or evaluating a system. A common pitfall is trusting undocumented data; the guidance component exists precisely because reliability of sources varies.
tiers.paperLevel: Bird and Simons (2003) characterize language resources as data (information documenting or describing a language, from unanalyzed recordings to fully annotated texts and descriptive grammars), tools (computational resources for creating, viewing, querying or otherwise using language data), and advice (information about which data sources are reliable).

explainer.example: A team building a transcription system collects annotated speech recordings (data), a query tool for viewing them (tool), and notes on which archives are trustworthy (advice).
